newsitem.title: USA: Chilly weather does little to cool Mardi Gras.
newsitem.headline: Chilly weather does little to cool Mardi Gras.

text.p: Chilly temperatures and cloudy skies had little impact on Mardi Gras madness on Monday as hundreds of thousands of revellers threw themselves into raucous non-stop parties and parades.
A 26-year-old Chicago tourist, who declined to give her name, wore a skimpy Las Vegas showgirl costume on top of a sweat suit and thermal underwear as she stood in the French Quarter Monday morning.

"I've been partying all night but I'm not crazy enough or drunk enough yet to wear these sequins and feathers without something under it," she said, waving a drink in a plastic cup. "Hey, look for me tomorrow, it might be different."

"These parades are something else," said her companion, another first-time Mardi Gras reveller. "I've never seen anything like it. They throw all this stuff at the crowds from these huge floats and people fight for it but nobody really gets hurt. Awesome!"

Mardi Gras runs from Jan. 6, Twelfth Night, to Fat Tuesday, the last day of debauchery before the Christian observance of Lent begins on Ash Wednesday. The major celebration, with costumes ranging from cosy Dalmation suits to a handful of feathers and a few bits of leather, moved into high gear Friday night and continues through Tuesday.

One New Orleans police officer said, "The only difference so far with the cooler weather is there seems to be a little less skin showing this year. Of course that could change as the level of alcohol consumption goes up -- it acts kind of like antifreeze."
The floats are lighted, multistoried creations embelished with fanciful papier-mache figures towed along the streets behind tractors.

The "stuff" being thrown -- tons of plastic beads, rubber spears, bikini panties, aluminum doubloons, colourful foil-wrapped condoms, dolls and drinking cups -- is paid for by masked and costumed float riders, members of the Carnival krewes, as parade clubs are called.
The Mardi Gras influence is so strong that virtually all parades in the city are interactive, with watchers begging for favours and paraders dispensing them.

Except for the hospitality industry and public safety agencies, most business and governmental activities yield to general festivities on Mardi Gras. Even U.S. Postal Service carriers, dedicated to persevering through rain, sleet, snow and dark of night, give it up for the day.

"Deliver mail on Mardi Gras? You got to be kidding!" a Postal Service spokewsoman told Reuters. "We may try to get out some Express Mail, if it's going to a place we can get to through the crowds. But for the rest, forget it."
